title: Soil thin section

definition.text: A slice of rock, mineral or soil ground to about 30 μm and mounted on glass for study under a polarizing microscope.

facts.text: Soil micromorphology describes far more in thin sections viewed with a petrographic polarizing light microscope than a 10x hand lens can show.
Between crossed polarizing filters the minerals' optical properties alter the colour and intensity of light, so most rock-forming minerals can be identified.
Thickness is checked with the Michel-Lévy interference colour chart, usually with quartz as the gauge.
Thin sections reveal the relation of a material's components to one another, features often invisible in a hand specimen.
Paleosols are identified partly from thin sections: at least 60% recognizable pyroclastic fragments marks an Andisol paleosol.
Humus-form horizons have been characterized on thin soil sections by micromorphologists.

definition.text: Soil fabric made by organisms, typically small, often pelleted micro- and mesobiofabric left by ants, worms and termites and seen with a hand lens or in soil thin sections.

facts.text: As originally defined, a biomantle must show at least 50% biofabric.
Burrowing vertebrates and tree uprooting make coarser megabiofabric, cloddy surface spoil heaps for which the 50% criterion is moot.

title: Mineral alteration in thin section

definition.text: The changes natural processes make to a mineral's chemical composition or crystal structure, as they appear under the microscope.

facts.text: In thin section some minerals such as feldspar decompose readily and turn turbid, quartz stays fresh and clear, and others yield characteristic secondary products.
Alteration is governed by thermodynamics under the prevailing conditions, with water the most common and influential catalyst.

notes: Phrase concept (Mineral weathering in thin section); Optical mineralogy has no soil sentences.

title: Soil micromorphology

definition.text: The description, measurement and interpretation of soil features too small to see with the unaided eye.

facts.text: Work may begin in the field with a 10x hand lens, but much more is seen in thin sections under a petrographic polarizing microscope.
A recognized technique for some 50 years, it spread from pedogenic and paleosol studies to the soils and sediments of archaeological sites.
Micromorphologists have characterized humus-form horizons on thin soil sections.

definition.text: Polarized light microscopy covers optical microscopy techniques that illuminate a sample with polarized light, most useful on birefringent samples.

facts.text: A polarizing plate converts natural light into polarized light, and birefringent samples interact strongly with it, giving contrast against the background.
It is used extensively in optical mineralogy, the basis of identifying minerals in thin sections.
More complex variants include differential interference contrast and interference reflection microscopy.

title: X-ray microtomography

definition.text: X-ray microtomography uses X-rays to make cross-sections of an object at micrometre pixel size and rebuild a 3D model without destroying the sample.

facts.text: Also called micro-CT, it is computed tomography in which the sample rotates while source and detector stay still, or the source and detector rotate around the specimen.
Cone-beam systems use a 2D detector to record projection images from which cross-sections are reconstructed.
Stacking slices builds a volume of voxels that can be viewed in any plane, and segmentation separates structures that have similar density.
In geology it is used to analyze micropores in reservoir rocks.

notes: Page has no soil text; included as the non-destructive 3D pore-imaging method named in micromorphology context; soil use rests on the pore/geology sentence only.

definition.text: Image analysis extracts meaningful information from images, mainly digital ones, by digital image processing.

facts.text: Computers are indispensable for large data and quantitative extraction, but human vision still cannot be replaced in many applications.
Object-based analysis groups pixels into homogeneous objects by segmentation and then classifies them; over-segmentation is often preferred when classifying high-resolution images.
It is applied in metallography, for instance to determine the mineral content of a rock sample.
